note_tweet.text:
Global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026. This is based on the latest preliminary estimates from the Global Carbon Project, published today.

This is a small reduction within an overall upward trend. Emissions have grown more slowly over the past decade than in previous decades, but they have not yet peaked or begun a consistent decline.

This fall mostly came from a reduction in oil consumption and a small decline in gas. Coal use increased slightly.

Among the major emitters, emissions are projected to fall in China, the United States, the European Union, and Japan. But they’re expected to increase by around 4% in India.

Why did emissions fall? The authors cite three key factors.

The deployment of clean energy (particularly solar and wind) displaced some fossil fuel use that would have otherwise been required to meet growing energy demand. Electric vehicles also reduced oil demand. Finally, the war in Iran and its impact on oil prices led to reduced demand, which has inadvertently reduced emissions.

Emissions from land-use change are more uncertain but are projected to increase this year due to peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia.

note_tweet.text:
We have updated our topic page on migration!

Hundreds of millions of people live in a country that is different from the one where they were born. In some countries, the majority of the population was born abroad.

International migration can affect both the countries people leave and move to. For example, remittances (money sent back to family or friends by immigrants) can be an important source of income in their country of origin. In destination countries, migration can fill employment and skills gaps and contribute to economic growth.

But migration is also among the top concerns for the public in many countries. In politics, it is often divisive and controversial. People are often concerned about the effects on jobs and employment, public services, crime, and local culture.

Understanding these benefits and challenges requires us to first have a clear picture of migration itself. This page provides a starting point, with writing, data, and visualizations on the global scale of international migration.

On this new version of our topic page, we first look at the types of migration people often think of when the term comes up: irregular or illegal migration. We move on to international migration overall: residents, annual flows, and the number of asylum seekers and refugees. We then look at the demographics of migrants and the scale of remittances — money migrants send to their countries of origin.

(This topic update was led by @_HannahRitchie, @EOrtizOspina, and Tuna Acisu.)
